newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-PIOLINE, SAMPRAS FACE WIMBLEDON SHOWDOWN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-PIOLINE, SAMPRAS FACE WIMBLEDON SHOWDOWN.

text.p: Cedric Pioline ensured a Frenchman in a Wimbledon men's final for the first time in over 50 years on Friday but will need to play the match of his life to stop Pete Sampras joining some of tennis's all-time greats.
The American world number one cruised past semifinal opponent Australian Todd Woodbridge in straight sets to move ever closer to his fourth title in five years at the All England Club.
Only two men have won more Wimbledon singles titles this century and Sampras can also climb to within two of Roy Emerson's remarkable record of 12 career Grand Slam victories.

His 7-0 head-to-head advantage over Pioline, including a straight sets victory in the 1993 U.S. Open final, tells its own story yet the top seed will be wary of the way in which the Frenchman ended former champion Michael Stich's Wimbledon career 6-7 6-2 6-1 5-7 6-4 in the second semifinal.

Ranked 44th in the world, Pioline could not make it past the last 32 on his native clay at Roland Garros this year, but fully deserved to become his country's first Wimbledon final representative since Yvon Petra, dressed in long trousers, won the title in 1946.

As Britain's Greg Rusedski discovered in the previous round, the 28-year-old has one of the best returns-of-serve in the business and his all-round play was equally sharp after Stich had taken the opening set 7-2 in the tie-break in 53 minutes.

The German, who has announced he will be retiring in September, felt he might be destined to win Wimbledon this year on the grounds that his previous success, in 1991, also came in a rain-affected year.
But he grew increasingly frustrated as the match slipped away from him in the second and third sets and only won the fourth on sheer desire.
His wife Jessica could hardly bear to watch the final set and Pioline's camp were equally nervous, knowing their man had not won a five-set match for almost four years.

The Frenchman, who had treatment on an injured shoulder during the match, wobbled in the closing stages, particularly when Stich had two break points to draw level at 4-4. But he hung on to win in just under three hours to set up a final which he hopes will settle a few old scores with Sampras.
"I'm so happy I won, but I'm tired of this man, he's beaten me so many times," he admitted.
"In the U.S. Open final I lost in straight sets but maybe it's my turn this time. If I keep playing like this, who knows?"
Stich wished his opponent well. "I've played Cedric many times but I've never seen him play so well," he said.
Sampras's 6-2 6-1 7-6 victory over Woodbridge was summed up by one particular point in which the top seed slipped, fell over backwards, regained his feet and still won the point.

Although Woodbridge became only the second player this fortnight to take a service game off the American, who had put together a sequence of 97 unbroken games since his first round match against Swede Mikael Tillstrom, the result was never in doubt.

"Today I played one of the greatest players who was playing great," the Australian doubles specialist said afterwards. "His second serve is what sets him apart from other players. He places it on a dime."
Sampras acknowledged he was probably serving better than at any time in his career.
"I don't remember a Wimbledon when I've served as well as I've served this year. I mean, I've only lost my serve a couple of times," he said.
"I am a little bit fatigued because I've played every day since Monday. I'm looking forward to a day off."
